utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, on Thursday, the 25th of February, 2010, I would like to greet General Petkovic, first of all, the accused, the Defence teams, the OTP, and everyone else assisting us. Before I give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, there's a request for additional time for his cross-examination. I have been informed of certain developments of the issue that concerns two bulbs for General Praljak, two bulbs that he needs so that he can read his documents at night. The administration of the Detention Unit at this Tribunal has said that the detainees are provided with equipment -- with such items only in the morning, not in the evening, and as a result General Praljak wasn't provided with these two bulbs. I don't know if someone managed to get through the window or -- whether he was able to get some light through the window in order to see the documents, to read the documents, but that's all I can tell you. That's the information we have. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. As I understand it, yesterday the Trial Chamber invited the parties to make submissions concerning any additional time that they may wish to have for cross-examination purposes. And as I understand, I did see one motion. I don't know if others have filed motions. I thought, however, that perhaps this might be an issue that might want to be resolved at this point in time, before we commence with our cross-examination. I, myself, would like some additional time, 10 or 15 minutes, somewhere in that neighbourhood, but I believe others have asked for as much as an hour in addition to what was required. So that was the matter that I wanted to bring up to the Court's attention at this point in time, but I'm at your disposal. I'll proceed, if you wish me to proceed. Or if others want to be heard at this point in time, it might be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you should have 36 minutes, so you want another 15 minutes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Something in that neighbourhood, just to be on the safe side, Your Honour. I don't intend to do anything extensive with respect to the general. We do have some things that need to be clarified, so that's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll ask my colleagues. But General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think 36 minutes, on the basis of 6 hours, but as Ms. Alaburic had an additional 20 minutes, that's an extra four minutes per Defence team. So 40 minutes would be the basis, I believe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask my colleagues whether they agree that we should grant Mr. Karnavas an additional 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's not a problem. Mr. Karnavas, you will have the additional time you have requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it I can proceed, then. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First, I just want to ask you one particular question that came up during Judge Antonetti's questioning, when he specifically was going through the various accused. And in asking you a question concretely about Dr. Jadranko Prlic, I noticed that when you answered, you indicated that the executive authority -- the executive council, did not have any authority over the military in any direct fashion. But I want to go back and ask you the question that was originally asked by Judge Antonetti, and that is: Did Dr. Jadranko Prlic, in person, did he have any control over the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Jadranko Prlic did not personally have any control over the Main Staff, but he did through his intermediaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he give you any orders?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for specific orders, no specific orders were issued by Jadranko Prlic to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he give you -- did he give you any operative orders, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jadranko Prlic didn't give operative orders to me. The operative part should have gone through the authorities, through the Defence Department, and then it should have been conveyed to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the supreme commander again was who?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Boban had the right and had the authority to give operative orders?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He did so?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, he did so often bypassing you or the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did he inform you in advance that he was going to be issuing an order or did you learn of it thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wouldn't be such information, because otherwise the procedure would have been completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we heard testimony from a particular witness under the pseudonym of BF, and he came here and testified sometime in 2008. I believe it was September. And he indicated -- there was a discussion concerning the 18 April 1993 meeting that took place in Mostar. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that meeting very well. It was chaired by General Pellnas, Mr. Thebault, and another representative whose name I can't remember. The political representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Granic, was there, Mr. Boras, Mr. Prlic, and I attended that meeting too. As for whether any other lower-ranking officials were there, I can't remember. I also forgot to mention Pasalic from the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, as I understand it, you showed up at the meeting with Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Is that correct? You arrived together?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Prlic had to pass by the Main Staff, and he said that in order to avoid using two cars, I should accompany him. And we arrived in front of the hospital in his car, and that is where the meeting was being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that's what I want to speak about. So the fact that you arrived with Dr. Jadranko Prlic was not because he was in charge of you or you were his subordinate, but, rather, he was merely giving you a ride and you both showed up at the same time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Jadranko Prlic, in that context, represented our delegation. That's the information we received from Zagreb, information as to who would be part of the delegation. And he gave me a lift so that we could avoid using two cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "from Zagreb," I'm thinking of Boban, who was in Zagreb at the time. I wouldn't want you to take this differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll move on to some other matters that I wanted to discuss. And we met prior to coming -- prior to your testimony; is that correct? I came to visit you at the UNDU, with consultation with your attorney?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ms. Tomanovic was there, as well as Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the two of you and my counsel and myself. There were four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So just to make sure that the record is correct, it was Ms. Tomanovic, who is my co-counsel, and your counsel, Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Tomanovic, yourself, Ms. Alaburic and myself. As far as I can remember, the four of us. I didn't see a fifth person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to correct the record. There are no trick questions here. And during that time, we presented you with some transcripts of videos and asked you to look at them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The purpose for asking you to look at those transcripts was to see whether you had any familiarity with the videos; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When I had a look at the transcripts, I remembered the time and the context within which certain things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that's the purpose now of the following few questions that I have. If we could -- we'll go to the first video, which is dated 17 August 1992, and this is 1D02078. 1D02078. I'm just going to play the first segment just for purposes of seeing whether you can recognise -- we're going to listen to just a couple of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can stop right here. Apparently there's no translation. Now, for purposes of this questioning, we did provide transcripts, both in English and in B/C/S, to Your Honours - everyone else should have them - and also to the translation booths. So I don't know why there's no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel give the interpreters a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. My error. That would have been page 1 of 1D02078. I don't think it's necessary for us to re-listen to it, but it's basically the first paragraph, where there's an introduction, and we ended where the gentleman is describing the purpose -- you know, what he proposes: "I propose that we start by viewing a video-clip..." And so on. That's where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have found it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My question is: General, do you recognise this video-clip? And if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I recognise this video-clip. It was the second time these participants appeared in this programme. I can see people I know, the journalist Sagolj to the left. Mr. Pelivan is there. That was the first time I saw him over the TV. I hadn't seen him live before. Mr. Soljic in the white shirt, I know him. Mr. Prlic, I met him. Mr. Mariofil Ljubic, and the last person is Mr. Ignac Kostroman. But Mr. Pelivan and Mr. Ljubic were representatives of the Croatian people at the time in the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall when you saw this video? Was it when it was aired or sometime thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this discussion was broadcast through the Zagreb Television studio. I believe that this was broadcast from a studio in Split, this particular clip was broadcast through a studio in Split. I just assume that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the second segment, and this would be on page 4 on the English copy, and it would be on page 7 of the B/C/S for those who are helping us out in the booth. If we could show that second segment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The HVO is a civilian authority, the temporary authority of the HZ-HB. That should be clear. There is an overlapping of terms. The HVO is also used for military units that work in this area, and the same term is the term used for the temporary authorities. The temporary executive authorities were selected by the Presidencies -- or the War Presidents of municipalities, so in this matter the legitimacy has been assured of that temporary executive authority. In all its documents, it states that these are temporary acts, it takes temporary decisions, it respects the laws of the republics. "And in the preamble of all those decisions, it refers to decisions concerning the introduction of the state of war, the imminent threat of war, and to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. All the documents, all the headings, feature the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in no case should it be taken to be, and this is very often stressed, that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna means a certain break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In no case -- I believe that it constitutes one road -- one direction towards sustaining the statehood of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the materialisation of the interests of the Croatian and other constituent peoples living in it in an equal manner."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, having heard what Dr. Jadranko Prlic said back then, which would have been August 17, 1992, was that your understanding as far as the difference between the HVO and the HVO HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's what I, too, said at the beginning. I first wondered what the HVO one was, what the other HVO was, and then I understood that the HVO was civilian authorities and then you have HVO as a military authority. I also knew that the civilian authorities, and Herceg-Bosna as a whole, was created because of the military state of war, the imminent state of war, because of the state of war, as I said, and it was necessary to organise for the defence of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in places where the Croats were in the majority. Those were some of the duties of the leadership of the Croats. It's also correct that in all briefs, memorandums, you have the heading "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and reference was made to certain provisions of the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could look at the next segment, and that would be on page 6 in the English version and page 9 on the B/C/S version. And I want to make sure that the Trial Chamber understands that I've selected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to interrupt you the rhythm of your cross-examination, but perhaps it would be useful. Following Mr. Prlic's intervention, there's a journalist -- the journalist who returns to the issue of the legitimacy or illegality of Herceg-Bosna, and Mr. Kostroman responds to that. So that could be of interest. If you like, we could perhaps listen to what Mr. Kostroman has to say. It might be of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I was just about to say, Your Honours, that because of time limitations, I've had to edit and edit and edit, and I don't want to give the impression that we're being selective in what we're trying to present, because we're going to be forwarding for admission the entire video. But I think that would be good, and that's -- I believe it's immediately following what Mr. Prlic has said. So if you could play -- continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Mr. Kostroman, often also the Croatian representatives in the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina say that Herceg-Bosna is illegal and illegitimate. "Well, the basic cause of the disagreement between existing authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council and the organs of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna lies precisely in the lack of preparedness --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Apparently no one is getting any translation. I had to use a time-out signal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He played basket [as interpreted] in his youth, Mr. Karnavas played basketball in his youth, so he wants us to stop and then proceed and stop. Yes, the interpreters wanted to have the reference. It's page 5. It's after what Mr. Prlic said. The journalist then puts a question. The interpreters, therefore, have the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll start again where we left off. There's no sound now. There's no sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Well, the basic cause of the disagreement between the existing authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council and the organs of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna lies precisely in the lack of preparedness of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its organs for this war. Evidently, this war caught the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina unprepared, as if it had come out of the blue, as if it had not been obvious as to what was going on. And this is simply incomprehensible that a week before the start of the war, the president of the state should have stated that the army was the only guarantor of peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this is where the basic causes of all that is happening should be looked for. However, the Croatian Defence Council did not wait, like others did in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to see what would happen, and we had been preparing for this war before. And it is precisely our readiness, even before the start of this war, that resulted in the free areas of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And the result of everything that is happening now is that we are ahead of the Bosnia and Herzegovina authorities."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, did you want to pose a question or should I pose the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you've heard Mr. Kostroman's claim that he supported the documents, and Mr. Prlic and Mr. Kostroman didn't have any papers in front of them from which they were reading, so the answers were direct, as far as I heard, because as you may well imagine, I have just come to know about this document, and I have the impression that Mr. Kostroman is saying the following: He's saying that President Izetbegovic, one week prior to the declaration of a state of war, said, There is an army, and he seems to be discovering the moon, whereas the HVO had been preparing itself for a long time. So he says that there is a distortion between the authorities of Herzegovina and the HVO -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, which would be linked to the declaration of a state of war, and this justifies, in his opinion, the fact that the HVO is legitimate and legal. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first, when reference is made here to the fact that the president of state, Mr. Izetbegovic, says that the army is the only guarantor of peace, well, at the time President Izetbegovic thought that the army in question was the JNA, that they would guarantee the peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and General Pokanjac (phoen) would also guarantee the peace, as the main commander. So he believed that at the time the JNA would really guarantee the peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the army that Izetbegovic had faith in. And these are the misunderstandings that occurred when trying to understand how the army would act. It was a difference in understanding between Izetbegovic and the Croatian authorities. And finally that very same army, a few days later, the army he had faith in, detained him at the Sarajevo Airport. That was the problem. He believed in the JNA. The Croatian leadership said, Don't believe in them, don't have faith in them. What happened in Croatian Slovenia will happen here, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise to Mr. Karnavas for the interruption, but a technical or a date matter. I think, unless I misunderstood, which is always possible, the date given for this transcript -- or this event that's being recorded is, I think, in April of 1992, it was said at one point --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 17 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 17 August. And I believe it should be -- I would suggest, based on the context and some of the things that are being said, and the positions of these people, that this is 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe -- well, I believe, Your Honour, and I'll just put it -- it's perhaps further checking, but I believe that further investigation would show that this is dated in 1993. Mr. Prlic refers to being elected president the day before, and he was elected president in August of 1993, at least of the republic. But I'll stand to be corrected, but perhaps Mr. Karnavas can assist us further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist, because I think you're wrong by a whole year. This was in 1992, and all of this applies to 1992 and the beginning of the organisation of the defence of parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when Mr. Izetbegovic publicly states that the JNA was the guarantor of peace and stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless I am mistaken, in the document there is an indisputable material point. When the journalist introduces the participants, he says that Mr. Prlic was elected on Friday. Therefore, this must be -- Mr. Registrar, when I say something of importance, as if by chance things stop working. I shall repeat myself. Is it okay now? Yes. I'm repeating. In the transcript that we have of the interview, the journalist who is present, the one who is interviewing Mr. Pelivan, et cetera, and with regard to Mr. Prlic, he says that he was elected on Friday and that this is his first interview or appearance. So it cannot be any other date except August 1992. Do you agree, General Petkovic, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, it is August 1992, two days after Mr. Prlic was elected to his post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record, there is P00429, which is the appointment of Dr. Jadranko Prlic at that post. I don't want to go to it now, but for the record it's there for everyone to see. Now, if we continue on to the next segment, which would have been on page 6. This is -- we'll skip what Mr. Pelivan has to say and go to page 6. And I believe I indicated that would be page 9 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I think that things are clear. We must make it clear also to the people who are watching television this evening. "We very often have long talks, et cetera. I do not want to be a pragmatic man. If Bosnia and Herzegovina could have been politically resolved, this war would not have happened. Therefore, the self-same people who were supposed to resolve the situation before the war and evidently today and after this war are unable to solve it, and that is why Europe and the United Nations got involved to help solve the political problems in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "A constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina was also drawn up, which is quite clear, and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna fully respects the proposal of the Constitution. And as for those who do not want to talk about it and believe that by exhaustion, procrastination, a problem can be solved, I think that it cannot. We have to organise everyday life. Our economic, financial, and every other system in Bosnia-Herzegovina have collapsed. We all have to be clear on that with exceptional efforts, with numerous victims. More than 100 people from Mostar are undergoing treatment here and enabling [indiscernible] alone, so many have been killed, liberating us from the occupation in a part of our region. We had to organise life. Now, we have to make a road to Central Bosnia, for when winter comes, those people will not be able to get food. "So we have to work and at the same time negotiate politically. I believe that the points of departure formulated by Europe, stating that there exists three national units in BH and which clearly said and proposed which competencies those three national units should have, which rights should be assured to peoples in those national units, must be taken as points of departure for talks. "I believe that a very important question tonight, also to which we may or may not give an answer, is whether all in Bosnia and Herzegovina are anxious to see the war stop. My assessment is that not all are keen on the war stopping."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, General, this road that Dr. Jadranko Prlic speaks of in Central Bosnia, a road to Central Bosnia for the food to get there for the winter, was that road ever built?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that road was built across Vran Planina, and it is known as "Salvation Road," and that was the only secure link of Herzegovina with Central Bosnia. That is, going from Croatia across Herzegovina, one could reach the then free areas of Central Bosnia. Without that road, it would have been very difficult, in some cases quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please assist us. Was it the authorities in Sarajevo that built the road or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the construction of the road was taken upon itself by the authorities of the -- of Herceg-Bosna, and I think mostly construction companies from Grude did the work, and some from Siroki Brijeg, Posusje joined in. This was a major initiative to build a road across one of the highest mountains in the area so that vehicles carrying humanitarian aid and people from Central Bosnia could cross Herzegovina and go on to Croatia, and from there to Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Sarajevo authorities, and when I speak of that, I'm speaking of the president of the Presidency or the government that Mr. Pelivan was the head of, whether they made any financial contributions?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one gave anything, and I think for a long time no one paid these work organisations from Herzegovina, with the exception that the HVO provided the gas and minimum daily allowances for these people. So the construction was at the expense of the HVO or, rather, at the expense of companies in Western Herzegovina, and the central government did not make any donations for this road and learnt about its construction later, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The beneficiaries of this road, were they strictly Croat, or did other peoples, and I'm speaking of Muslims, in particular, benefit from the construction of that road?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, they had benefit from the construction of that road, both Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia, and this means the whole area as far as Tuzla and Eastern Bosnia, because that was the only road that one could take safely to reach Central Bosnia, the Tuzla region, and even Sarajevo. Convoys were directed via Kiseljak and other places to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to the next segment, and that is on page 12 of the English version and 19 on the B/C/S version. It's a very short clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, do you intend to come back to some of these pages later or are you moving straightaway to page 12, and you will not be asking any questions on the previous pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Regrettably, Your Honour, because of time limitations, I will not. However, if the Trial Chamber wishes, after I finish this segment, if the Trial Chambers wishes to go in to a particular segment, we could find it. So I don't -- as I indicated, I intend to admit the entire video. I just don't have the time, and I didn't feel it appropriate to ask for two or three hours for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have a question, and during my time. General Petkovic, it is a shame that I discover this document now. It's really a pity. I'm looking at the list of participants in this interview, and I put myself in the place of the viewers or listeners hearing the interview. We're in August 1992. It is Croatian Television, apparently, in Split, and the TV viewers note that there is the prime minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Pelivan, and they also note there is the vice-president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and also representatives of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and its president, who has just been elected, Mr. Prlic. So they might think that all the persons present represent the political vision of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But looking at the document, I focused on what Mr. Pelivan was going to say, who is the prime minister, who is, after all, the legal authority, quite legal authority. And perhaps it would be important to hear what he says about the question of the HVO, its competencies, its zone of influence, et cetera. Could we look at the video and listen to what Mr. Pelivan says?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I take it you're referring to page 8 in the English version. Is that where it would begin, or -- is that the segment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm referring to page 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. We could go back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when he speaks about the regional organisation, referring to economic and cultural issues. It could be interesting to know what the official prime minister says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. So this would be at page 6, Your Honours, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There was the question of constituent units or regions, and to be quite sincere, you have frequently talked about regions rather than constituent units, and one has the impression that among representatives of the Croatian people, this question has not been fully resolved. What is the problem with these constituent units? "I think that there should be no problem, if we analyse what is best suited in respect of the organising of each people into constituent units. In fact, we did not conduct sufficient joint talks on this topic, so that in some respects things remain unclear and insufficiently defined. "First of all, the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina is such that it requires regional organisation of both economic flows and geographic areas and the cultural entities. Therefore, the regional form of organisation should not be disregarded, being widely known in the world, and one giving very important practical results. That means that we should not, at the very outset of talks, negate the possibility of the existence of regional organising, provided that in all areas there can feature a different degree or percentage of representation of an individual people in that area, and the defining category is the majority share of a people in a given region. "And as regards constituent units, I personally feel that constituent units should be constructed so that the sum of the regions makes up a whole in which the constituent units of each people is constituted, which then should, at that level, organise the manner of managing the overall interests of the people."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. LiveNote has gone down for a number of people in the courtroom in the last couple of minutes. May I just mention that so that it could be resolved as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems a problem with the transcript. Everyone has the text in front of them. You have heard the comments by Mr. Pelivan. General Petkovic, what would you say regarding his vision of these regional areas in which all the peoples would be represented? What would be your comment regarding his remarks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pelivan first mentions that regional organisation is absolutely legal with respect to many questions important for life, in this specific case for defence as well. Also, Mr. Pelivan points out that constituent units should be formed as a sum of those regions, and I think that he's referring to the already well-known Cutileiro Plan which envisaged such constituent units. And in my view, Mr. Pelivan, as the representative of the government, has nothing against. On the contrary, he supports regional development and the formation of constituent units, but he says that there should be further talks about these things so that many points can be co-ordinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to Mr. Karnavas for intervening, and of course this is not his time, but I do have to make a record here, Your Honour, in light of the time issue, because I think what's happening now illustrates perfectly the dilemma for various parties in the courtroom, including the Prosecution. And, again, my concern here is not personal to Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Karnavas is simply proceeding to the current arrangement, so I'm not throwing any stones whatsoever in Mr. Karnavas' direction. But the way things are playing out here, as I say, is a perfect illustration of the problem. Now, the road to Central Bosnia, as an example, is a new topic. It's a new topic, hasn't been raised before. It's been added to the case. Now we're talking about Mr. Pelivan and his role in the BiH government at the time; also, not previously a topic in the case. Brand-new topics, among other examples. I picked those two now. There's already been several others this morning. Then Mr. Karnavas, rightly so, says, Well, I don't have time to cover the entire transcript, because he's constrained by time-limits, just as the other parties are and just as I am. So when he says, Well, I can't have time -- don't have time to cover it, perhaps you would like to cover it, Your Honour, then you cover those issues, you raise new issues in the case, and then presumably I'm not going to be given any additional time to deal with these new issues. Now, that's the fundamental problem of the way that things are working here and the time elements. To date, we've had about something like 24 hours of examination, raising all sorts of issues, and I'm counting, I'm counting, and there's no way the Prosecution -- I'm just going to continue to make my record. There is no way the Prosecution, in six hours, can possibly begin to respond to all the issues that are being raised. And when Mr. Karnavas, rightly so, says, Well, I don't have time to go into this, and he has to exercise his judgement, just as all the parties do, and just like I would have to, in theory, exercise judgement and skip time, but then it's brought back into the case by the Judge's questions, Well, let me ask it for you, Mr. Karnavas, in effect. And I'm not given any time to deal with that. So I'm making the issue on a number of points. There are new issues being raised. Mr. Karnavas can do that, according to the Chamber's guide-lines, new issues being raised, not part of Ms. Alaburic's direct, and there's the issue of time. And if new issues are being raised and if the Chamber is going into issues, and Mr. Karnavas says, Well, I don't have time to get into that, then that is to the detriment of the other co-accused and to the Prosecution if we are not provided time to also deal with that. And I'll continue to make a record on this, Your Honour, because I'm going to ask -- I will tell the Chamber, I'm going to ask for additional time -- substantial additional time to conduct the Prosecution's cross-examination. And I'll continue with my -- I apologise to Mr. Karnavas for my interruption. Again, it's not his time, but I'm going to continue to make this record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I will give you the floor, as it was I who put the question. I discover, in a few seconds -- I don't need hours. In a few seconds, I discover that the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this name has already been heard here in the documents or uttered by witnesses, that he's intervening regarding the question of regional organisation. It's a subject that is not new, because it has already been embarked upon. And this question of regional organisation stems from the Constitution, so it's not new. As it's not a new subject, I only need a few seconds to put my question, that's all. And I asked the witness what he thinks of Mr. Pelivan's comments on regional organisation. The witness answered also in a few seconds. And you, Mr. Prosecutor, you need a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do, and I think it's, with all due respect, completely unfair to say what you just said. It has nothing to do with whether there's a topic that's been raised in this case. Surely, in the past four years -- in the past four years, virtually all sorts of topics have been raised. That's not the test. And if that's the test, then it's a test that is meaningless. The question is what's gone into with a particular witness, and as Mr. Karnavas has just demonstrated properly, he doesn't have time to cover every possible topic, even though it may have been raised in April 2008 or November 2009. It hasn't been raised with this witness, and it's the time with this witness that controls. And it's completely unfair to say, Well, in a couple of seconds, I could do this. Well, maybe, maybe not, but we've just spent at least the last 10 minutes on a new topic. Now, I'm going to ask for to have the same additional 10 minutes to be add to my time. And I'm going to continue to make this record and I apologise if that offends anyone, but this is fundamentally unfair to parties; the co-accused and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deliberate and perhaps will grant you additional time. I, personally, see no problem with that. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just so that there are no more interruptions, or fewer, we could consider this as a running objection on the part of the Prosecution, and then perhaps afterwards you could just list the new areas. You know, to quote Don Corleone in "The Godfather," Everybody around here knows I'm a reasonable person, I just want to try to get through this as quickly as possible. So if we could go to page 12 in the transcript, and I believe I indicated it was page 19 in the B/C/S. It's a short segment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Their sons have been killed, and we can deal with those questions in the future. Concretely, what fault do you find with the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example, for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?" Prlic: "I do not know even know what they did over these four months so that I do not know what fault I could find with them or what I could approve, for indeed nothing of it was reflected on the ground. I was in Mostar all the time of the war, in connection with the decisions adopted at the level of the republic. I know that all information as to what was happening in the area of Herceg-Bosna, in particular Mostar, was accorded marginal significance. "You know, for example, that the name of the Armed Forces of BH was changed five times in the start; that in the first variant the Yugoslav People's Army was within the composition of the Territorial Defence; that the aggressor was named only after a month or a month and a half after the aggression; that only on the 6th of August, the HVO was actually legally proclaimed a component part of the Armed Forces of BH. I really do not know what the decisions were. We did not get them because of the communications blockade, so that I cannot have a position. "Precisely owing to that overall blockade, we were compelled, people living in that area and who had earlier held some jobs in that government, to try and organise that government and for it to try and restore life."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, General Petkovic, earlier on you did mention, I believe it was to the President's question, the fact that Izetbegovic was relying on the JNA to come to the rescue of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But from what Dr. Jadranko Prlic is stating, is this correct, keeping in mind the time-frame?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, obviously it was not correct. And Mr. Izetbegovic, himself, realised this and felt it. I have a feeling that when he personally felt the consequences, when the JNA was -- arrested and subjected him to a certain kind of torture, that only then he realised what the JNA was. And that is when the people, the Bosniaks, started to establish the first units to resist and oppose the JNA, and that was too late. Therefore, the role of army in Bosnia and Herzegovina was not realised in time. It was viewed as a protector of BH. He even felt that a part of that army would stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina and proclaim itself the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was completely erroneous on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is Dr. Jadranko Prlic correct when he states that the name of the Armed Forces of BiH had changed? And if so, to what extent did that play a role in the psychology of the Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as their safety and as far as their comfort with respect to being protected by the state authorities of BiH?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is no doubt that the Croats didn't feel comfortable when Mr. Izetbegovic says, It is our army and it will protect us. The Croats couldn't believe that, and they were simply afraid of such positions of the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Furthermore, Mr. Izetbegovic decided that the army he was forming should be called "The Territorial Defence." As the Territorial Defence was the defence of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then all of this was taken away from those peoples and everything was given to the Serb people and the JNA, and this caused frustrations among the Croats, why a territorial defence. Again, it is part -- it was part of the armed forces of the former state. And, finally, that is when Mr. Boban decided that the Croats, of whom he's the commander, could not be called in any other way except "the Croatian Defence Council," and let the others call themselves as they wish. And he reproached Izetbegovic, why he opted for this term "Territorial Defence," because the association of the people was something bad. And two months later, he changed the name from Territorial Defence to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to page 20, that clip on page 20, the next clip, and this is the last one for this. And this should be 31 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Do not think I'm being malicious, but please, Mr. Prlic, as the president of the HVO, do you know that credits for armaments are being sought abroad?" "No, but the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna --" There is too much interference and static. "No, but the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna has sent a request, a conclusion that we'll submit to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to request a third of the resources for Herceg-Bosna. Otherwise, it does not want to be responsible for those resources and leaves itself leeway to take appropriate and countermeasures. Also, I think that foreign borrowing should be resorted to both for the needs of the defence, of the feeding the population, and for reviving economic flows. I think that it is time something was done, because so far, to be frank, we have been speaking about the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. "Up to now in the defence actions of the Croatian Defence Council, the republic has only had a negative role. Let me be quite frank. Practically not a single combatant of the Croatian Defence Council got even a single tea bag from the republic. The people themselves provided all this for their combatants and the combatants themselves provided this, but we're ready to talk based on the principles I've just spoken about."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I didn't compare the translations, but I know that something that Dr. Prlic said was wrongly translated in lines 14 and 15. Dr. Prlic said, Let us speak about the republic and Herceg-Bosna, which means the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna. This way, it turns out that it was only Herceg-Bosna that was discussed, which was formed a year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Going back to the question, itself, about credits for armaments, do you know whether Izetbegovic or the Sarajevo authorities actually obtained any credits for armaments or cash -- or financing for armaments from abroad?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know about any credits, nor could I have known at that time that the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina raised any credits. But I did know that donations were coming in to them from various sources, especially from the Islamic world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, at least, what Dr. Jadranko Prlic is saying here is that Herceg-Bosna should also be receiving some of those resources because, after all, they are defending part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you know whether the HVO received any of the assistance, monetary assistance or armament assistance, that the Sarajevo authorities were receiving from the various Islamic countries or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. From the resources collected up at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its Presidency, I don't know who, on behalf of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army, collected those resources. None of that was siphoned down to assist the Croatian Defence Council. And Jadranko Prlic is right there when he says that, and he says not a single tea bag was sent for any soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That concludes my questions for this video. If we could go on to the next video, unless there are any questions; follow-up, that is. 1D02070. 1D02070, if we could just look at that. We may just look at part of it. It's a short clip. The first couple pages, I wanted to get your opinion on something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Croatia is again helping Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Makarska, Croatia arranged a meeting of the two governments and representatives of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The aim of the meeting was an agreement on free delivery of humanitarian aid throughout BH. Here is what the participants of the meeting told our colleague Ivo Sipek [phoen]: After a day of co-ordinating the work, the prime minister of the Republic of Croatia, Mate Ganic, earlier this evening, as the host and the witness, signed the agreement on the passage of humanitarian convoys. The deputy prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Hadzo Efendic, and the president of the Croatian Defence Council in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Jadranko Prlic, signed it, determined to implement it. "Their signatures are witnessed by the International Committee of the Red Cross, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, and UNPROFOR should quickly easy the troubles of Croats [indiscernible] -- within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Croatia is the initiator, host, and witness. Croatia provided its good services, having gained experience during the entire war. "From its beginning until now, all humanitarian convoys travel from Zagreb to Knin and Topusko and everywhere else in complete freedom, because as far as respective international humanitarian law is concerned, the Croatian position is that it must be respected in full without any reservations. "This was actually the reason we invited both sides to come here and to reach this agreement. This position is fully supported by all international humanitarian organisations."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll stop here. The rest can be read, what we provided, even though I'm skipping what Dr. Jadranko Prlic indicated. For purposes of admission of this particular video, I want to ask you a couple of questions, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this particular meeting, this video, and the contents thereof?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do know about the meeting. It was a meeting in Makarska at the beginning of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the purpose of the meeting, if you might tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was about humanitarian aid and assistance, and the passage of humanitarian convoys and distributing it. I think this is an abridged version, it didn't encompass everything. As far as I heard, they discussed the quantities of humanitarian aid, what was intended for the Croats, what was intended for the Bosniaks. So this is just a brief excerpt. I don't think this was in the studio. This was the report of somebody who was in Makarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you know whether this agreement was adhered to by all sides?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no problems, no problems that couldn't be solved in providing humanitarian assistance. Now, the meeting was announced as being -- as a meeting to resolve the very great problems that existed. I don't think that was the case. I don't think there were any major problems. I think that somebody, through humanitarian aid, wanted to politicise the whole issue, because humanitarian convoys went into Makarska and they continued to go forward. So we were surprised why a meeting was being held to discuss humanitarian convoys and assistance, because the UNHCR and everybody else, UNPROFOR, had their plans to provide assistance according to their plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go on to the next video, which is 1D02230. 1D02230, and it's dated 21 September 1993. I'm just going to initially show the very first part and see whether you have any recollection of this one, for foundational purposes, before I go into any other segments.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The latest declaration from Geneva, signed by the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and the Muslim leader, Alija Izetbegovic, is just another piece of paper, or is it something else, the question is now. There is a saying that, Who has been bitten by snakes fears lizards as well, and the Croatian people have truly signed numerous pieces of paper with Izetbegovic thus far, so doubts are to be expected. After every signature, we have the same situation; massacre. After so many casualties, everything is too late."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall seeing this video-clipping? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this footage was broadcast several days after the declaration between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic was signed, and I think it was signed on the 14th of September, 1993. So this footage was shown in a -- within a programme some seven or eight days later, because there was a lot of talk about the declaration. So it was interesting to see what the participants at the meeting thought about the declaration, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you recall seeing it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Well, let me tell you, these programmes that were broadcast in this way, with representatives taking part from executive and political power in Herceg-Bosna, people liked to see programmes like that because you could see what your representative thought, because Mr. Prlic and others couldn't go to 10 different places in one day. So this was a good opportunity to convey the necessary information. And the importance of the declaration between Tudjman and Izetbegovic was such that a lot of attention was paid to the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And incidentally, Your Honours, the general is referring to P05051. That's an exhibit already, the declaration, itself. So if we go to the first segment, and that would be on page 2 in the English version, and I believe it's page 2 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Greetings from Neum. Marhaba [phoen] was never president, nor will it ever be in Neum. A bit of humour at the beginning. "So the basic question tonight is: What after the signing of the declaration? As we said in the introduction, this was the most important topic discussed between the special envoy of the president of the Republic of Croatia, the foreign minister, and the vice-president of the government, Dr. Mate Granic, and the leadership of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as a "trojka" together with several additional ministers. "Mr. Prlic, can you tell us at the beginning, and please answer this question that has been asked frequently yesterday, why are Croats discussing the implementation of the declaration, while the Muslims, it was reported, on the eve of the Central News, especially yesterday, are attacking Croatian areas and citizens on all fronts? "The Croatian side shall implement every document signed authorised representatives of the Croatian people, and this has never been an issue. It is obvious that in implementing this declaration, the level of implementation should also depend on the level of willingness of the other side to implement this document. It is, nevertheless, necessary to point out at the beginning that we will never do anything to the detriment of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina through implementing any document. So we are prepared to implement it fully, we are prepared to make the first step in every area, and I made this very clear yesterday. But the second step will not be made until the other side does the same."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you tell what is Dr. Jadranko Prlic speaking about at this particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Prlic is obviously speaking about the way in which the declaration should be effected, the declaration signed seven or eight days previously, and he says that the HVO will implement the declaration, but we'll also see what the other side is doing about it, that is to say, the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, prior to the question -- or prior to the answer, I should say, the question was prefaced with some information concerning attacks and ongoing conflict with the Muslims. Do you recall what was happening on the ground at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to remind you that in this courtroom -- well, the declaration was signed on the 14th, and we, in this courtroom, on several occasions introduced the document from the 4th Corps commander dated the 15th of September, preparing a broad-scale operation of taking control of Mostar. And I'd like to add to that that on the 15th, I think it was, the declaration was signed between the Serbs and the Muslims, and in one of the items it says that it was their joint interest to have an exit to the sea, so that on the 15th, that is to say, just one day after the declaration, we have an order from the BH Army, and we saw Pasalic's order and the sector commander's order, we saw it two or three times in this courtroom - I don't know what the numbers of those documents were - and the operations were launched to take control of Mostar. And I think that that is why Journalist Bowen was brought in to give the news first that the BH Army had taken Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And before we go to the next segment, my colleague, Ms. Tomanovic, tells me that the declaration that the general just spoke of was 3D00451. That's the Karadzic-Izetbegovic declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that correct? You're shaking your head, General. That means yes?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, sorry. Just to avoid confusion, without looking at that particular document, just on date, is this -- we are talking about 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're into 1993 at this point. And if we go to the next segment, which is on page 3 in the English version, page 4 in the B/C/S. It's a very short segment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Let's continue our discussion with our guest. Mr. Prlic, briefly, how do you interpret these activities of the Muslims in attacking all areas, all locations, as was said at the meeting yesterday, on the Croatian Defence Council?" "This is a well known and classical pattern of behaviour for the Muslim side which is practically buying time in situations they think it is possible for them to achieve their goals in the field. Objectively, those percentages of territory that were set as a precondition for the Muslim side to sign, they want to realise in the field as soon as possible, and primarily on those areas inhabited by Croats and the Croatian Defence Council. However, neither the declaration nor any other document that regulates international war law and International Humanitarian Law does not prevent anyone from defending themselves, and we must be ready to defend all the territories within the lines where we are located now. We must seek political solutions, but also, as was said at the beginning of this programme, we must be prepared to respond and guard our territories. We must, first of all, be realistic when considering anything. There are certain issues the cause of which a positive effect might be created in the public, and this also has to be taken into account. This is part of special warfare and the entire package of war activities. But let me emphasise again we must be realistic. "The Muslim Army in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina is an enemy army, as far as the Croatian Defence Council is concerned, and all talks, agreements, and negotiations are exactly that, only negotiations. This actually suits the position of the Croatian Defence Council and the government, since it is in line with the latest decision. Seven or eight months ago, we sent a letter to the Mission of the European Communities, the Monitoring Mission of the EC, stating that we're ready to negotiate with the Serbian and Muslim governments - this was eight months ago - on all open questions and the functioning of these infrastructure systems, education, et cetera. And I can reiterate this today: That we're open and ready to talk, because we believe that even in the throws of the fiercest hostilities, it's always necessary to talk with the enemy."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, General, here Dr. Jadranko Prlic characterises the Muslim Army in Central Bosnia - he restricts his answer to that - as an enemy army. Would you agree or disagree with that statement? And if so, please explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but the general received a slightly different interpretation to Mr. Karnavas' question. It wasn't quite as Mr. Karnavas put it. So to avoid a misunderstanding in the answer, I'll repeat and say that Mr. Karnavas said that Dr. Jadranko Prlic characterises the Muslim Army in Central Bosnia, he's asked about, and he was limiting this just to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, let me answer that question and observation. We're dealing with the end of September 1993, the 21st of September, in actual fact, when they were holding this discussion, and that's the time, as we saw yesterday when we looked at the maps, what happened to towns in Central Bosnia at that time, and the HVO and the BH Army, and the problems involved. Jadranko Prlic knows that at the end of September, the Muslims had taken control of Travnik, expelled the Croats; took control of Fojnica, expelled the Croats; took Bugojno, expelled the Croats; and took 99 per cent of Konjic municipality, expelling the Croats. Jadranko Prlic knows this full well, so he can have no other attitude towards an army that expelled over 100.000 Croats than the position he takes. Similarly, I believe that Jadranko Prlic also had in mind the fact that this was a time of the Neretva 93 operation which was fierce and moving towards the town of Mostar, that is to say, Mostar municipality, and moving down towards the coast, the sea. So Jadranko Prlic was fully informed about everything that was taking place in Central Bosnia at the time. He had the Office of Refugees informing him and everybody else informing him about the plight of the 100.000 Croats who were seeking salvation in different ways and means, so he knew that we had been expelled from many towns. How, then -- how else can we describe an army that did this to us but to say that it was an enemy army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to page 6, the next segment, and in the Croatian version it would be -- I'll find it in a second here. It's rather long. It's on page 8. My apologies for not being --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We often read in here that Muslim politics and policies are crazy. This is just an illustration of our arrogance when we speak of this. These are not crazy politics at all. It's a very well-thought-out politics. Almost every step has been planned, and political, military, and propaganda activities have all been co-ordinated as a whole. If we analyse the activities from the beginning of the war, then we can very easily come to that conclusion. "All negotiations and stalling were just a means of buying time. The Muslim side, headed by Alija Izetbegovic, has used the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina entirely for its own purposes. All embassies and consular offices, diplomatic representative offices, are manned by people of Muslim ethnicity, who promote the Muslim idea and the interests of the Muslim people. Of course, whether these are truly the interests of the Muslim people is debatable. "There is also the issue of their leader, Alija Izetbegovic. I can say that it was also Croatian politics that, to a large degree, created Alija Izetbegovic, who didn't have support, nor does he today, in the Tuzla region, where relations between Croats and Muslims are, so to speak, bearable in the Zazine region. But I do believe that extremism will become more widespread in these regions, because the longer the war lasts, the extreme viewpoints and behaviour also become stronger. "I think that one of the great mistakes made by Croatian politics was leaving Alija Izetbegovic in the position of president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He took advantage of this position and strengthened it in the field. He managed to combine what only seemed to be two opposite fractions in the Muslim people. One of my qualifications was that the Muslim nation was a fundamentalist core which was negligent [as interpreted] at the beginning, 1 or 2 per cent of the population. The majority were the so-called moderate Muslims with a European orientation, and a smaller group of Jugo-unitarians. The core of this group was composed of former Yugoslav officers. Through the efforts of the BH Army, these two groups merged, the fundamentalists and the Ju go-unitarian stream, and the modern European people of the Muslim people objectively had no space to survive. It became smaller and smaller. Most of the people from this group left Bosnia and Herzegovina, and some later sociological research will probably give a better assessment than I am able to do in these few minutes. "But to go back to your question, it is not a question of whether it's a crazy policy and politics or not. It can be called so if we observe it in the long term. But short term, it will give certain results. However, it is in the interests of the world, and I want you to understand why these declarations are being signed in the first place. Regardless of how difficult it is to talk about these times, yesterday 20 soldiers were killed in Mostar and 73 wounded. It is very difficult to talk about officials of the Croatian people, of some future co-operation, calming of relations, and the situation. However, we must understand one thing. It is in the interests of the world that this Muslim republic within the future union of Bosnia and Herzegovina have a European orientation, thus be a secular state similar to Turkey, and show the world that it is possible to have one more such state, apart from Turkey. It is considered that this Muslim republic would be what the world wants to see, and if this is to be so, this path must lead through Croatia. "So these are some strategic interests. There are a million things that intertwine, and many are frequently parallel, yet manage to collide. But in creating strategic policy, all this must be taken into account, and still that what I have been talking about must not lose its basic importance; the defence of the Croatian people, regardless of where they live in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, General, this is September 1993. By this point, is it not a fact that there is talk of having three republics? That's the plan that the internationals are pushing for Bosnia-Herzegovina, three republics within a Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, three republics as part of a union of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And finally maps were drawn up to depict what this should look like. The representatives of the three peoples just had to accept this. And after all those negotiations and discussions, the war should have come to an end, but obviously that didn't happen. What Mr. Prlic has said, well, Mr. Izetbegovic thought that the union of Bosnia and Herzegovina given to the Bosnian side could be extended through war, because territory taken through military means were included in the map that related to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. What Alija took was given to him in that plan. And in addition, the Stolac area that was given to the HVO was taken and given to him. So his appetites increased, quite certainly. He wanted the whole of Central Bosnia for himself, and he wanted access to the sea. And perhaps he would just give the Croats Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the assessment that Dr. Jadranko Prlic makes of Alija Izetbegovic, that is -- or his side, that they're stalling, that's a fact, that they were stalling precisely because of what you indicated; they were trying to get as much territory -- occupy as much territory? Therefore, at the negotiating table, that would be their point of departure, to keep and control what they had? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I'll give you an example. Mr. Izetbegovic sent Delic, a new commander, on the 10th of June to speak to me about Travnik. He knew that Travnik, in 24 hours, would fall. But let's accept that that's correct, too. Izetbegovic, on the 15th of June, wrote to me and Delic and said, Put an end to the war, but he had already launched an action in the direction of Kakanj. So what are we discussing, then? Some papers had to be drafted to cover up, but in the field instructions were being followed. And after seven or eight towns taken by him in Central Bosnia, well, naturally he didn't say, That's enough, we'll stop there. He continued; Busovaca, Vitez, Kiseljak had to be dealt with, and the entire territory of Central Bosnia would remain in the hands of the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, usually this is our time for a break. I have two or three -- three, actually, small segments, but I -- perhaps we could take the break now and get to those segments, or I can continue. I'm up to your -- I'm up to whatever you decide. I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the end of the interpretation. The Registrar has told me that you have used up the time allocated to you, but you have just said that you have two or three additional clips to show, and this would mean that you'd be asking for additional time. How much additional time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, by the looks of it, Your Honours, and maybe I miscalculated, I don't think more than 15 minutes. There are just two -- three clips. One is a little bit longer than the others. I've timed them. The timing of them is less than five minutes altogether, but then there are questions. So we could take the break now, and if you decide to give me more time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but just a minute. I will ask my colleagues whether they agree to grant you 15 additional minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have 15 additional minutes. We'll have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, the Chamber will render two oral decisions with regard to time. One will be somewhat lengthy. Oral decision on the request for additional time to conduct the cross-examination of Witness 92 ter NO and with regard to the allocation of time for the hearing of this witness. In a request dated the 1st of February, 2010, the Prosecution requested four hours for its cross-examination of the Witness NO. The Coric Defence responded to this request on the 2nd of February, 2010, and the Praljak Defence made an identical request on the 3rd of February, 2010. On the 3rd of February, 2010, the Prosecution filed a request for leave to respond, and this request was accompanied by a -- the said response. On the 3rd of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence requested an hour to conduct its cross-examination of the Witness NO. The Coric Defence responded to the request on the 15th of February, 2010. The Chamber authorised the Petkovic Defence to file a response in an oral decision dated the 16th of February, 2010. This response was filed on the 17th of February, 2010. Finally, in a request dated the 5th of February, 2010, the Stojic Defence requested 18 minutes in total for its cross-examination of Witness NO. In addition, it requested that the additional time requested be charged to the total time allocated to it by the Chamber. The Coric Defence responded to this request on the 15th of February, 2010. The Chamber notes that all these submissions were filed under seal. Witness NO, called by the Coric Defence, is to be heard pursuant to Rule 92 ter on the 15th of March, 2010. The Coric Defence informed the Chamber and the parties of its intention to conduct its examination-in-chief for the duration of 30 minutes. The Chamber notes, in addition, that Witness NO was initially supposed to be a 65 ter witness for the Coric Defence and was to be heard viva voce for two hours in the course of examination-in-chief. The Trial Chamber hereby decides to authorise the filing of a Prosecution response. The Chamber would like to point out that with regard to allocating time for the cross-examination of a witness who is appearing pursuant to Rule 92 ter, as a general rule, it allocates this time on the basis of the time that was initially requested for the witness in the witness's capacity as a viva voce witness, and also on the basis of distribution of the time that is available as stated in Guide-line 5 of the decision of the 24th of April, 2008. Given such practice, given the submissions of the parties and the 65 ter summary for the Witness NO, the Chamber hereby decides the following. I will read this out slowly so that there are no subsequent requests for clarification. 1. The Coric Defence will have 30 minutes for its examination-in-chief. The Stojic Defence request shall be granted -- I would prefer to see "1" and "2" in the transcript. So, 2, I'll repeat what I said. 2. The Stojic Defence request shall be granted, and they will have 18 minutes to conduct their cross-examination. The Chamber also takes note of the request from the Stojic Defence to have the additional time of six minutes charged to its total time. 3. Thirty minutes shall be granted to the Petkovic Defence for its cross-examination with regard to the subjects that this Defence team intends to deal with through this witness. 4. The Prosecution shall be allocated two hours for its cross-examination, and this time is equivalent to the time that had initially been planned for the Coric Defence for its examination-in-chief. The Chamber will now also render an oral decision on the time allocated to the Defence teams for the cross-examination of General Petkovic. First of all, as far as the Prlic Defence is concerned, the Chamber, in addition to the 40 minutes that it had a right to, granted it 15 minutes this morning, and further to a following request, a new request, granted it an additional 15 minutes, which means that in total, 40 minutes plus 30 minutes will have been allocated to that Defence team. That makes a total of 100 [as interpreted] minutes. As far as the Stojic Defence is concerned, the Chamber -- 40 and 30, that's 70, not 100. So one hour and ten minutes, an hour and ten minutes. As far as the Stojic Defence is concerned, the Chamber hereby allocates to the Stojic Defence one hour and ten minutes in total, an hour and ten minutes. For the Praljak Defence, the Chamber hereby allocates an hour and 20 minutes to that Defence team. With regard to the Coric Defence, the Chamber hereby allocates that Defence team an hour and ten minutes in total. This is a unanimous decision, but I personally would like to say the following: I fully agree with the decision made by the various Defence teams, part of which had to do with the consequences of Judges putting questions. With regard to that particular issue, I would like to point out that the questions that I put to General Petkovic were almost identical to the ones -- almost identical to the ones that I put to General Praljak. And unless I am mistaken, I didn't have the impression that any new subjects had been dealt with in my questions. But whatever the case may be, I am inclined to grant additional time for the Defence teams that believe that they require such time. Mr. Karnavas, so you have your 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go on to the next segment. That would be on page 9 in the English version, on page 12 in the B/C/S version. So 9 in the English version, for our friends both in the English and the French booths, and 12 -- page 12 in the B/C/S version. It's a small clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Mr. Prlic, let's return to what was said at the meeting yesterday. It said that the humanitarian convoy, regardless of everything else, have to pass through. Could you comment on that?" "Many questions are asked about that that shouldn't even be commented on. Either we're filling in time or having meetings, certain subjects are imposed just to exact pressure on the Croatian side. The English would say, It's out of the question, we don't want to discuss such matters. Neum shows the objective position that Croatia and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are facing, so if we are speaking about that, it shows what our objective position is and the pressure exerted on us from the world.
