"The humanitarian convoy -- humanitarian convoys were never a problem. Their passage through Herceg-Bosna was never a problem, never. It's an artificial dilemma that has been created around this issue. There was never a problem concerning this, not in positional behaviour. "In any case, who built roads in these mountains of Herzegovina, if not the Croatian Defence Council? And they have been the only means of communication and entrance for humanitarian aid and commercial goods, ammunition, arms, and everything else into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These roads served as an exit way for over 60.000 refugees from all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so this doesn't exist as an issue at all. "Who was it, then, who used this issue of humanitarian convoys for political purposes, and why, if what I'm implying is correct? As to whether there were individual cases, yes, probably so. We even investigated some; for instance, one that was on Sky News and concerned the convoy of four petrol tanks that left from Metkovic and arrived at our border. The military police wanted to make a routine inspection that was arranged in the procedure, in accordance with the procedure. However, UNPROFOR didn't want to allow the tanks to be inspected. They just ordered them back. And as a result, a problem was created. "For us, this doesn't amount to a problem. Nothing will be allowed to travel through the territory of Herceg-Bosna without having undergone the normal and previously-arranged inspection of goods. "This very clear principle was also accepted by UNPROFOR and the High Commissioner for Refugees, and regarding this yesterday they emphasised, you heard during the meetings, the representatives -- if UNHCR said that there were no problems regarding the passage of humanitarian convoys. The objective problems now are the intense war activities on all fronts, and especially in Central Bosnia and the area of Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: General, my question is: Here Dr. Jadranko Prlic is talking about one particular instance concerning the inspection of tanks, and he gives the impression that there had been an agreement with the internationals, in particular UNPROFOR and the High Commission for Refugees, that such inspections would be legitimate and appropriate; is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, that is correct, and it was agreed at the level where you agree about the passage of convoys. There was a goods or transport list that was compiled. I think that's what it's called. So you have such a list, a freight list. It says, such and such goods are going to be transported. Then you would inspect it, and they would be let through. That was it. No one asked for the goods to be unloaded and to be viewed. They just had a look at the freight list. It would say, You have authority to pass through, and that's how things happened. That was the only means of control, as far as I know, that had been agreed on, and that was at the border. I think this is a quite normal procedure. You show the freight list, the bill of lading, the list of goods, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you spoke of a border, and we see here "Metkovic." Some of us do know where Metkovic is, but which border are you and, in particular, Dr. Jadranko Prlic speaking about ?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border of the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because if oil was being transported, it would be from Ploce, and the UNHCR had its warehouse in Metkovic, in Croatia, and moved from there to Bosnia and Herzegovina through the Valley of Neretva. This is the route they used. So the warehouses were in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, warehouses for oil and food, and control was -- well, it was controlled at the border with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that the name of the border crossing is Doljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And Ploce is in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, a technical question. I'm not intervening, I'm not interrupting Mr. Karnavas' questions, but it's a technical question. You speak about these lorries being inspected, and you say this was done at the border. When I was listening to you, I thought about what I did 20, 30 years ago, because as a prosecutor I was responsible for the motorway in Northern France, where many vehicles and lorries passed through, lorries from Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, and so on and so forth, so I was familiar with all these problems, I dealt with all these problems. And when listening to you, I wondered whether you wanted to say that when a lorry arrived at the border, there was a customs inspection, and then there could be a stamp that shows that the contents were inspected, and after that has been done the lorry can circulate, it can't be controlled, but when you see that it has already been inspected, the goods aren't checked. But perhaps in your system that you are describing, there was a control at the border, but there was no customs immunity for the vehicles when circulating, so the HVO could have another look at the goods being transported at certain check-points, control points. Is that what you are telling us, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Customs didn't inspect humanitarian goods, especially if it was under the UNHCR, if the UNHCR had organised this, and other organisations responsible for such things. So such goods weren't inspected by Customs. In Metkovic, in the UNHCR base, there was an HVO representative. Such an agreement had been reached, and this representative would supervise the loading of goods. At the border, you'd only show a piece of paper on which it said "Four lorries," such and such a number of tonnes of flour, and so on and so forth. No one had the look at the contents of the lorry. You just had that so-called bill of lading. I think that's the term. You'd see that it was loaded in Metkovic and that it should now have free passage. Nothing else was controlled. The Customs didn't do anything else because they didn't have the right to impose duty on goods of a humanitarian kind. Customs service was concerned with commercial goods. And this procedure took no more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that in Metkovic, all the lorries had a letter list which described the goods being transported, and when the HVO inspected the lorry or, rather, controlled the lorry, in fact, they just had a look at this letter, this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, I apologise, but I have now understood what the witness was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I had asked the question, but it was not recorded for some reason. Ploce. Ploce is in Croatia, it's a deep-water port, in fact; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Ploce is a town and a port in the Republic of Croatia, and it has an oil base, it has a certain capacity, and it was used for transporting oil there, and oil would then be transported from that place to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Neum, which is a little bit further up and in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, also is a port town, we could call it that, but it's not a deep-water -- it does not have the capacity that Ploce has; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neum is in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, Neum was never a commercial port. It was a port for small boats that the local people used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we can go to the next segment. That would be on page 24 in the English version, and it's page 36 on the B/C/S version. So it's page 24, English; 36, B/C/S. Again, it's just a short clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Thank you. Let's move on with other questions. "Are you aware of the cry for help from the Croats from Zenica? This is a question from Stipo Viskovic from Switzerland, and it's a question for Mr. Prlic. "We are fully aware of this. We are well informed. And to the extent that this is possible, of course, it is difficult to have all the relevant information from Zenica which is objectively under a blockade. "The position of Croats is very difficult, especially the position of those who have been captured. Mr. Jukic spoke of this a bit earlier. Six months prior to these intense conflicts in Central Bosnia, we anticipated these developments, especially after the arrest of the brigade commander and the beginning of the conflict in Zenica and the situation in Cagljas, et cetera. We asked for a corridor to be opened to save the brigade and the inhabitants of the area, because it was easy to anticipate what would happen next. However, none of the international organisations, UNPROFOR, the UNHCR, for example, wanted to support us in this, so they are giving no support today either."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, General, first of all, Dr. Prlic is talking about an arrest of a brigade commander. Are you aware of this incident? And if so, could you please tell us who the brigade commander was?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I'm aware of this. It was Mr. Zivko Totic, the commander of the Zenica Brigade. He was arrested on the 15th of April, 1993, together with four members of his escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall about what time that would have been? What's the time-frame? We know that this video here is in September 21, 1993, so can you give us a time-frame?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said the arrest of Zivko Totic and his escort occurred on the 15th of April, 1993, but the imprisonment of members of the HVO brigade, there were two in Zenica, started from the 16th and continued for a few days. At the same time, during that period some of the Croats who were in suburbs of Zenica, closer to the Lasva or Busovaca Valley, they were expelled mostly to Busovaca and Vitez. However, some of them remained. No one knew who was taking care of them, or how, and assistance was requested from the UNHCR and other international organisations, assistance to determine what the situation was. Although they didn't have the possibility of living under normal conditions, they should be moved to Busovaca, where the others were, or a guarantee should be provided for them so that it would be possible for them to live there, because in Zenica, in the -- from the 16th and 17th, the system in Zenica had broken down. There was no one you could rely on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Dr. Jadranko Prlic speaks of a corridor, and I want to tie this in with the notion that we've heard from the Prosecution and we see in the indictment, that there was this allegation of reverse ethnic cleansing, the Croats wanting to cleanse certain areas where Croats are, get them out, expel them, if you will, in order to have them re-populate; in other words, making Central Bosnian -- turning them into Herzegovinians, if that is possible. But that's -- my question goes to whether there was such a policy, whether Dr. Jadranko Prlic is talking about a corridor for those purposes, for the reverse ethnic cleansing, Croats cleansing themselves.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honours, whether the inhabitants -- the Croatian inhabitants of Central Bosnia, well, you would know that they would never leave their areas unless they were forced to by such a force. The Croats from Central Bosnia were very much tied to the areas in which they lived. Therefore, Jadranko was trying to find a way to move Croats to the closest safe place, to move them there from the Zenica area, and settling Croats in Herzegovina wasn't necessary. Herzegovina was mostly Croatian, and those people really didn't want to leave their areas because they were never really tied to Herzegovina. It's interesting that a few people from Central Bosnia, even in peacetime, tried to go and live in Herzegovina. No, they didn't really move in the direction of Herzegovina, and they weren't delighted with the atmosphere in Herzegovina, so to speak, so they didn't want to go there. They preferred going abroad. It's not that they didn't like Herzegovina, but that place was a place where the atmosphere was quite different to the atmosphere in the areas that they inhabited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And since we're speaking about Zenica, this is the place, is it not, where the Mujahedin were more or less headquartered out of or at least concentrated to a great extent?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Zenica was the headquarters of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH. It was the greatest base, with the greatest number of soldiers. And the Mujahedin who gathered in Central Bosnia, well, their centre was also in Zenica, but they would select certain places on the periphery of Zenica because they wanted to remain isolated. They didn't want others to have access to them. So Zenica was their destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And isn't it a fact, General, you having lived through that period, that the Mujahedin instilled fear with some of their tactics and approaches, such as beheadings?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, and such acts had an influence on the security of those people. Naturally, they were fearful, and they asked for protection, you know. But when someone cuts off your arm, you don't have protection, you don't know who will protect you, and our brigades had been practically cut off in those areas -- had been practically imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll go to the next and the very last segment. It's very, very short. It's page 25 in the English version. So it would be the following in the English version, and I believe it's 37 in the B/C/S. It's a very short segment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Let's go on to the next question. What will happen to the Croats in Tuzla? A viewer from Trbovlje has this question for Mr. Prlic. "From the very beginning, our principles have been clear. Once the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established on a legal system, that it made it what it was. The Croats in Tuzla will have all the rights the Muslims will have in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and it is through mutual agreements of the two republics, Croatian and Muslim, that as of tomorrow we will attempt to protect the full rights of the Croatian people in that area that will remain outside the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, General, Jadranko Prlic here is speaking about what was envisaged, to have three different republics in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Your Honours. This was the concept of three republics within the framework of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was known as the union of republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And essentially here what he is saying, and, in fact, mirrors what was on the table a year earlier or so in the Cutileiro Plan, that members of another ethnic composition or constituent peoples would have the same rights and same protections, no matter what republic they would be residing in; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the conditions, one of the requirements. Everyone had to have the same right, regardless of numerical strength of the Croats, for instance, in the Tuzla region, or the Bosniaks in a region where the Croats were in the majority; that is, the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. That is how it was called in the union of republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Tuzla would have been in the Muslim republic. I think we saw a document - I don't have the number right now - where they had a draft of, I believe it was called "The Republic of Bosnia," but that would have been in the Muslim republic, correct, Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. Tuzla, not just the town of Tuzla but the entire Tuzla basin, was to belong to the republic that was called at first the Bosna, and that is the Muslim or Bosniak republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions. And, Your Honours, I wish to thank you very, very much for extending me the time. If you wish to have any questions. I do wish to point one point out, and that is, going back to what you indicated earlier, Mr. President, that you had wished you had this before, I hate to bring up a sore subject, but I have attempted six times to do this in other videos. And I just mention this because perhaps after today you might wish -- I don't want to revisit the issue without some sort of permission, lest there be further consequences. But, in any event, I believe we saw a demonstration of how some videos that we have presented do, indeed, have exculpatory value and may be of great assistance to the Trial Chamber, particularly since these were the words of at least my client at the time of the events, where the entire public could see. And the Prosecutor, of course, is free to argue whatever he wishes, but our position is those were the positions held by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, they were forward-looking and they were European-looking, and they were tolerant in every which way. So thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before giving the floor to the other Defence counsel for their cross-examination, my understanding was that Madam Alaburic had something to say. So I give her the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. I just have a small point to make. We have promised not to contact General Petkovic, and we have observed that promise from the moment he made his solemn declaration. But the Prosecution has given me a document as new disclosure and said that they intend to use this document in their cross-examination. Since it is a document that I have never discussed with General Petkovic, and I don't know whether he's familiar with it, I would ask your leave to contact General Petkovic for two minutes during the next break to show him this document and ask him two questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me confer with my colleagues, whether they agree. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to say the Prosecution has no objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution agrees that Ms. Alaburic can discuss it with General Petkovic. Everyone is in agreement, my colleagues too, so you can discuss this document in a moment. After D1, normally it's D2. I don't know whether they wish to begin now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We would, indeed, like to begin. Could the usher please come to my friend Mr. Khan to take over the binders for this examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [In English] Sorry, sorry, it's the same binder. One for Ms. Alaburic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, I will follow this binder in order. As I didn't get as much time as I hoped, so I will have to leave out some things, but I hope that we will finish during the day. I would like to start with a topic that my colleague Mr. Karnavas had asked you about. That is the meeting on the 18th of April that was chaired by Mr. Pellnas, and he spoke about this on page 49521, lines 3 to 14. And for that purpose, I wish to show you the first document, P2016. And what I wish to refer to is page 4 in the Croatian and page 3 in the English version. I will tell you, just briefly, that it is stated here that on the 18th of April, a meeting was held, attended by Mr. Granic, the meeting that we have referred to several times, and that, as it is stated on the second page, the first meeting of the warring parties in Mostar was interrupted by the defence minister of the HVO, who said that an attack by the army had started in Central Bosnia of a large scope, and then the meeting was postponed. Mr. Petkovic, do you remember this meeting, and did Mr. Stojic interrupt the meeting, as is stated here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course I remember this meeting. It has been referred to with Mr. Prlic's counsel, the meeting of Mr. Pellnas and Mr. Thebault, Petkovic, Prlic, Granic, Boras. It is not true that Stojic interrupted the meeting. The meeting had already been completed, and myself and General Pellnas were looking at the room from the entrance. We were in the left part of the room. And with the help of an interpreter of the military observers, myself and the general discussed how we would continue work over Mostar and that he would try and let me know when exactly General Halilovic would arrive for these talks. I asked that he come, and Mr. Granic promised that he would contact Sarajevo for General Halilovic to come. The second group was to the right. I don't know what they were talking about. And that is when Mr. Stojic walked into the room and asked first, Where is Petkovic? And then he saw Mr. Granic, and he had a piece of paper in his hand. It was a report from Central Bosnia. And it was normal that he said, Mr. Granic, do you know what is now happening in Central Bosnia? Has anyone here mentioned what's going on in Central Bosnia? And that was Mr. Stojic's conversation with Mr. Granic. The latter, of course, said that he didn't know what was happening. Mr. Stojic then read out this document which had come from Central Bosnia. It was a report. And the question was put whether anything would be done to improve the situation in Central Bosnia. And that was all the conversation conducted in connection with Mr. Stojic's arrival at that meeting. There were no threats whatsoever by Mr. Stojic addressed at anyone. I did not notice that Mr. Granic felt afraid or in any other way affected, because after all, Mr. Stojic showed that document to me, too, I saw what it was about, and after that he left the hospital where the meeting was being held and he went to his office. And I stayed on for a while with General Pellnas and Mr. Thebault. For us, it was rather outside the hospital than inside when we discussed what we would be doing, especially when General Morillon and General Halilovic arrived. Let me just add, I didn't even notice straight away that Mr. Stojic had entered, because I was with General Pellnas. Had he shouted out, then certainly my attention would have been drawn towards Mr. Stojic and the group he had approached.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petkovic. I should just like to say that on page 61, 13, 62, third row, it says "Granic" instead of "Ganic." We are talking about Mr. Ganic, so as to avoid any error.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really apologise. I think each time I first said "Granic," and then "Ganic," but it is Ganic, the vice-president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have some problems with my teeth, so the R is a bit difficult to pronounce.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us forget the R when we are talking about Mr. Ganic, but let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But tell me, Mr. Petkovic, did Mr. Stojic have a pistol on him when he came in?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, Mr. Stojic, I never noticed him wearing a pistol. As far as I knew, he had a pistol in the front of his car, and it was his driver who was responsible for the pistol. I think we called him "Buca." Now, I don't know whether that was his name, or surname, or a nickname. Buca had two pistols and one in the car. I never saw a pistol on Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Ganic. After this meeting, did Mr. Ganic come again -- after this day when Mr. Stojic came, did Mr. Ganic come either to the premises of the Defence Department or the Main Staff headquarters, after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Ganic dropped in with Mr. Halilovic briefly to the Defence Department or the Main Staff. When coming to Mostar, General Morillon asked whether it would be a good idea for Halilovic to come and for us to be the hosts, and we said, Yes, and we spent a brief time there. And then Messrs. Ganic and Halilovic, together with General Morillon, went on to General Pasalic and stayed with him for a little longer. So they returned to Medjugorje without me, and my assessment is that they spent more than two hours talking to Mr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I'm asking you this because one of the witnesses in the courtroom here said that Mr. Ganic, after the alleged incursion of Mr. Stojic, was so frightened that he needed special security to reach Zenica. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Mr. Ganic travelled to Zenica in the same convoy as myself. I and Mr. Ganic, at the UNPROFOR base in Medjugorje, got onto the vehicles of the Spanish Battalion, travelled with them to Kiseljak. Then we moved to the vehicle of the Canadian Battalion, because that was their zone towards Zenica, and then via Visoko-Kakanj, we reached Zenica. And the whole evening, he attended the meeting that all of us attended, and Mr. Zubak accompanied him. And he was very active at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, we'll move on to another topic. So the next document is P1901. I shall briefly tell you that during Witness 4D-AA, page 49263, line 23 of the transcript, a witness for your Defence, when shown this document from Bruno Stojic, commented on it. And then we'll look at the next document as well. The next document is 2D3080. And then I'll ask you a question. This is information sent to the Administration of SIS of the HZ-HB on the 25th of April, 1993 -- I'm sorry, March, signed by the commander of SIS, reporting on problems connected with the HOS units in Livno. What is particularly important is that it says that this HOS unit was attached to the Petar Kresimir HVO Brigade and had become a component part of this brigade and was carrying out orders of this brigade, but that in this HOS unit certain tension and disagreements had arisen. And then on page 2, it is said that due to the newly-developed -- new developments, the head of the Defence Department, Mr. Stojic and yourself, are advised to call Stanko Brgoca [phoen], the commander of this brigade, Mato Sukan [phoen], for an interview to deal with the situation. Could you tell us, linked to the previous command of Mr. Stojic, dated the 16th of April, asking for this HOS brigade to be disbanded, do you remember what happened to this brigade, this HOS brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was not a brigade, first of all. They were called a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: A unit, a unit. Yes, I'm sorry, a unit.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of those men joined the Petar Kresimir Brigade, Petar Kresimir IV Brigade, and a smaller group of those men left Livno and went to Zagreb, as far as I can remember, the unit that was in Livno. However -- but regardless of that, problems arose among them again, and that is that their headquarters in Zagreb, Mr. Paraga, also tried to settle things among those men who had now joined the HVO, and I think this was done behind everybody's back. So he found some men that he was in touch with, and this was causing problems to the brigade commander in Livno. And we asked that this problem be dealt with, and we had a man - I don't know whether he's mentioned here. I can't remember his name. I think he was in Tomislavgrad; I'm not sure - who managed to deal with HOS in a special way, somehow to put some order there, that they had to fit into the brigade system, and that they couldn't do anything on their own initiative. And this gentleman helped a part of those troops so as not to be arrested and leaving for Zagreb. They were from this area, but they had Croatian citizenship. And that is how this problem was dealt with in Livno. However, something happened that we learnt about much later. I think they tricked us by saying that they were joining the brigade; whereas, in fact, they believed that they continued to be HOS. And even though they removed HOS insignia, perhaps they carried them in their pockets.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, that means that this order, issued by Mr. Stojic, P1901, came after these problems, but the situation was resolved peacefully ultimately; nobody was arrested or anything else. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was this great problem with them, but they tried to resolve it in a peaceful way by negotiating with them and, first of all, asking that they become included in the system that was already set up in the area, and that they couldn't play their own game and do what they wanted. I don't know how many there were, but, anyway, the brigade that had three and a half thousand men could not tolerate a group of not more than 30 or 40 combatants doing what they liked.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petkovic, for that exhaustive explanation and the information you've given us, but we'll have to be briefer to save time. Now look at 4D, please, 3418, the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I've just seen this document. The 16th of April, 1993, is the date. You know that there is the Prosecution claim according to which there was an ultimatum, and as of the 15th of April all units were to be either subordinated to the HVO or to the ABiH. When I see this document, I put the following question to myself: I want to know whether this document can support the Prosecution claim or not, the claim that as of the 15th of April, the HVO wanted to be the only master in Regions 3, 8, and 10, and as a result it instructs everyone to either join the HVO or to be disarmed. So can this document be linked to the HVO's desire to remain alone in Regions 3, 8, and 10, or is this just a coincidence because it concerned this unit that could present certain problems, and as a result the decision was taken to definitively separate from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, the HOS units, even if they -- well, they weren't tied in amongst themselves properly, and each of their groups, numbering 15 to 20 men, would control the area they were in according to their own volition. So at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, in Tomislavgrad and Livno, and anywhere elsewhere they happened to congregate, they never formed a single unit with 400 or 500 people rallied together so that you realise that it was a unit. No. They were small groups, 15, 20 men, and each of them had their own plan, and they would always be active in some settlement. They sold weapons, they engaged in crime, they caused excessive situations, and things like that. They were engaged in smuggling and so on. There were very few of them that were willing to go up to the front-line and hold the line. No, they had their own agenda, their own plan, which was to topple the system that existed, and to make as much nuisance of themselves as possible, and to try to impose themselves on others. They thought nothing of opening fire, or kidnapping somebody, or engaging in things like that. So I would call them a sort of wild group of men. And I encountered them in April 1992 for the first time in Tomislavgrad, when I had to go there to help put some reason into a group like that and to work under one command. So that was the way they acted and behaved. They were little groups that went into action far from the front-lines in little settlements. And wherever they came, they caused a lot of problems, especially as their leadership -- as their leader had gained certain positions in the Croatian Party of Rights at the time, and that party had lost a lot of sympathisers, so they wanted them, by hook or by crook, to impose themselves in the region in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, nobody had gained much advantage from them. It wasn't a large unit with 400 or 500 men. You would have little groups of 20 or 15 men, and they ran amok mostly. So what date was it that you said, the 15th, the 16th? And it had nothing to do with that. Everybody who accepted that remained. But let me say they left as a HOS because they pledged to be part of the HVO, but through their connections in Zagreb, nonetheless, they managed to remain HOS in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in your opinion, the date was just a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, without any intention to testify, but the witness did talk about this in 2D3080, the next document in line, and it says there that that particular unit, after the disbanding of HOS, did join up the HVO brigade which was named the Petar Kresimir Brigade, and it became just one of the brigade's units. So it wasn't -- even if there was an ultimatum to be re-subordinated, there was no need, because it was already part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Isn't that right, Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's the report of the 25th of March, 1993, that says that about Livno.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a brief question related to the H-O-S, HOS. You've told us about all the problems you had with them, but did they wear uniforms that were inappropriate and that caused you problems, for which you had to intervene on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. They wore black uniforms, and in their office or offices they had Ante Pavelic's photograph up on the wall, and things like that. So, as such, at the time they couldn't be considered combatants either for Bosnia-Herzegovina or anything else, for that matter. The main photograph that they each had in their office was Ante Pavelic's. That was what they liked to do, and also to wear black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's move on to another area now. I have given the number of the document. It is 4D00348. You've found the document, have you not, Mr. Petkovic? Now, this is a report from Mr. Miro Andric. It's signed. We see that it's a report for the period between the 13th of January to the 22nd of January. And in the beginning, Mr. Miro Andric says that: "Following a verbal order from the head of the Defence Department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, on the 12th of January, 1993," he says, "I went to carry out a mission in Prozor, with the objective of calming the situation down in Gornji Vakuf municipality." It is not my intention to look at the entire document. Mr. Miro Andric was in the Main Staff, was he not? And during the examination-in-chief, you explained what his position there was, and I'd just like to ask you now if you remember, where were you on the 12th of January? Could you tell us, or repeat it if you've already told us? And why was it necessary for Mr. Miro Andric to go to Gornji Vakuf at this particular point in time in the first time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're dealing with the 12th of January, when he left -- or, rather, when he received an order. He probably set out then. And I and Mr. Boban were still in Geneva. And on the evening of the 12th, we were on our way back to Croatia, and then I continued on my journey to Herceg-Bosna. And Mr. Stojic sent Andric to Prozor to join up with Colonel Siljeg and our negotiating team there, which was discussing matters with the BH Army through the mediation of BritBat in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, when you returned, did you hear anything about the fact the fact that the BH Army delegation had been expanded and that's why somebody had needed to go to the negotiations of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A delegation arrived -- well, at first it was a local Vakuf delegation which was later joined by - well, I don't know the exact number - three or four, and we have the names in the documents, a delegation of the 3rd Corps from Zenica, which means that a 3rd Corps delegation from Zenica also joined in. And I think they referred to themselves as the state delegation. Anyway, on the Bosniak side and the BH Army side, there was this local delegation led by the commander of the local brigade and some others, and then at a certain moment a delegation from the 3rd Corps of the BH Army arrived and joined in, too, from the superior institution, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, you say that you weren't there and that Mr. Boban wasn't there either; in Mostar, that is. Now, was that the reason why Mr. Andric went, because of this expanded delegation that arrived at the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that was why he was sent there, to strengthen our delegation or, rather, so that we should have a representative outside the local people who attended. So Colonel Siljeg arrived, and as we can see, Colonel Andric arrived, too, so that we had a two-level delegation, a local one and one of a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, fine. I'm now going to go on to another area, and for that would you look at document 2093, please, P2093. You have testified about this document, how the order came into being, and that was on page 49530 of the transcript, lines 1 to 3. You mentioned those negotiations. Now, we have before us an order, and you were supposed to sign it, but somebody signed in your stead. And it relates to a cease-fire and a cessation to hostilities agreement, and the resolution of the problem between the HVO and the BH Army, which was signed in Zagreb by Mr. Izetbegovic and Boban, as well as General Petkovic and Halilovic, along with the signature of Mr. Tudjman and Lord Owen. Now, what I'm interested in is this, Mr. Petkovic: We see here that there's a signature there, Mr. Stojic's signature, whether a facsimile or his signature. But tell me, anyway, we see that the document was issued at 8.00 a.m., so could you explain to Their Honours how it came about that another person signed for you and that Mr. Stojic signed a document of this kind?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was similar to the previous situation. At this point in time, Mr. Boban and I were still in Zagreb. An agreement had been signed, and we've seen it in this courtroom a number of times. And from Zagreb, they demanded that orders be issued straight away on the basis of the agreement; that is to say, that they shouldn't wait for Halilovic and me to arrive in Mostar and Sarajevo. But Zagreb called up and said that, in the spirit of the agreement that had been reached before our arrival, orders should be issued straight away in the meantime. And Bruno Stojic in that case did so, and he signed on behalf of the Defence department, and Zeljko Akrap signed on behalf of the Main Staff. So the demand that came in was, The agreement has been signed, follow it on and tell both commands and headquarters to issue orders for a cease-fire. So that's how this order came to be written while Mr. Boban and I were still in Zagreb and were on our way back. We came back in the afternoon. The first available flight from Zagreb to Split was at 1.00 or 2.00 p.m., and then from there we would go to Mostar and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, do you happen to remember whether you contacted Mr. Stojic and gave him instructions of this kind? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I can't remember who that was. Was it Mr. Boban or did I call him up? Anyway, the position was that the orders should be signed straight away and that on that very day the orders should be carried out; that is to say, that a stop should be put to the conflicts and a cease-fire enforced.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now let's look at another document of similar content. It's 2D3081, and it is another order issued by Mr. Sefer Halilovic this time. What I want you to focus on is the fact that he sent this order to the HVO Main Staff as well. Does that, Mr. Petkovic, indicate, and with the previous order we saw that it was received by the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This one was sent to the Main Staff of the HVO, so I'm going to ask you this: And Judge Antonetti asked you something like that, too. Was it a single army and just the two components of one and the same army, because these orders were being exchanged in this way?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was an agreement, and an attachment to the agreement was also signed which states that the HVO and the BH Army were the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is why it was requested that orders be issued straight away. Here I see that Halilovic signed it personally, which means that we signed our order 12 hours before Halilovic signed his, which means from Zagreb we phoned up Mostar, told them to issue the order. And Mr. Halilovic first of all flew in to Sarajevo, and then he proceeded to issue that order, so he lagged behind us at least 10 hours. And I know it was sometime around 1.00 or 2.00 that he flew to Sarajevo in an UNPROFOR plane, whereas we used the regular flight to Split and continued on from there to Mostar. But, anyway, the orders were issued as we had agreed. Who issued them first, well, we can see that. It would have been better had he phoned up from Zagreb, called Divjak or Siljeg or somebody else, and given them instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... 49151, line 24 -- I'll repeat this. I don't know whether you heard me. I said -- it's not in the transcript. I said that Witness 4D-AA has testified here, and on pages 49151 and 49.000 -- or up to 49155, on those pages he was asked about certain military issues by Judge Antonetti, about Vitezovi, about whose control it was under, what happened with the battalion. You have testified about this at length. You said quite a few witnesses mentioned under whose command it was. So my question is: Have a look at P2673, and then -- D2673 should be after this. Have you found it? First I'll ask you to confirm this again. The Vitezovi Battalion, during this period - we're speaking about the beginning of 1993 up until the 8th of June, 1993 - where was it based, and under whose command was it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vitezovi Battalion, Your Honours, at that time was in the territory of Central Bosnia. In particular, it was in the town of Vitez, or, rather, the municipality of Vitez. So that's in Vitez town. It was a battalion from the Main Staff, but it was attached to Commander Blaskic, the commander of the operative zone in Central Bosnia, and at that time it was still active in that role in the territory of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Here we can see an amendment on the mobilisation deployment here, mobilisation development. Item 2, it says the Vitezovi Battalion and Tvrtko II battalion, and then the code is mentioned for the unit. It says -- I'm sorry, let's start at the beginning. It says: "Put an end to the mobilisation development," and then it mentions the Vitezovi Battalion. Although this was signed by Mr. Stojic, do you remember, were you involved in this entire problem, and why did this occur?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Vitezovi Battalion was -- it wasn't very strong. The number of troops was reduced. At the beginning -- it didn't have many men at the beginning, but in all the fighting in Central Bosnia it was used -- well, if someone lost their position, they were sent in to take back the position. Many of them were wounded, they had many dead, so, in fact, the battalion could only exist as a battalion on paper. It could only be a battalion on paper. So there was a decision according to which -- as it wasn't being reinforced, people didn't want to report for service in that battalion because they saw that those people were really being used wherever others failed and lost the lines. So, as a result, they avoided going to that battalion, so a decision was taken to terminate the Vitezovi Battalion. On the 8th of June, such a decision was adopted according to which the Vitezovi Battalion should be terminated. And, similarly, the Tvrtko II Battalion was to be dismantled. And as far as Tvrtko II is concerned, they refused to sign -- its officers refused to sign the contract, but they wanted to be professionals without a contract. So that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the following document that comes, 2D002, which should confirm what you have just been saying. But there is one particular item I am interested in. I will draw your attention to that. Mr. Petkovic, this document, for certain technical reasons, does not bear a signature. It is from the Croatian Defence Council, from the command of the operative zone. It was forwarded to you and to Mr. Stojic. It should have been signed by Mr. Blaskic. Please assist us and tell us whether you can remember this document. Have you ever received it -- did you ever receive it, and was it sent by Mr. Blaskic? Here he says -- immediately after receiving the previous document on mobilisation development, he says that he saw officers and commanders from the Vitezovi Battalion who were unhappy because of certain terminology used, for insulting terminology used. It also says because of -- in the order according to which the independent Vitezovi Battalion is to be terminated, and this confirms that they actually received this. So here in this document, it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we get the number again? We seem to be having trouble.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D3082. It's the next document. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, what is most important with regard to the commander they were under is that it says: "I have to point out that the Vitezovi Battalion really carried out all military tasks assigned to it and that it was a guarantor of the professionalism, especially in certain combat activities. It bolsters morale and provides security for all fighters at the lines." Here, Mr. Petkovic, it says what you have just been saying, yourself, that up to then 780 or more were killed, 2.017 were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you. That doesn't have to do with the battalion. It has to do with the military zone as a whole, whereas the battalion, you've skipped something. It had 80 soldiers, and now it only has 40 today. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. General Petkovic, go three lines back.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. That's what you said. I just want to go through this. It says in the operative zone, we have had such and such a number of dead and wounded. And then further down, it says, I -- you, the chief of Defence, and you, the chief of the Main Staff, I have the following request from you, temporarily dismiss the order for reforming the Vitezovi Battalion and the Tvrtko Battalion. If possible, pay the remaining salaries. If possible, the Health Department should pay a cash advance to the staff of the Novi Bila Hospital. Mr. Petkovic, can you confirm that you also received this document from Mr. Blaskic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was addressed to me, and the heading, Your Honours, and after a decision according to which the Vitezovi Battalion was to be dismantled, this was Colonel Blaskic's reaction. He had immense praise for this battalion and for the important role it played in the defence of Central Bosnia, and a request was made not to dismantle the battalion. It was to continue existing, in spite of the fact that it had very few troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, in this request of his, did he explicitly state that the Vitezovi Battalion carried out all the military tasks assigned to it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that's what he says. Let me remind the Chamber that when I testified in the Blaskic case and was faced with such questions, I said that it was only in the Croatian newspapers that I discovered that the battalion was so bad. But, in fact, the situation was quite the contrary. So someone deliberately wanted to conduct a smear campaign against the battalion. I said that whenever I heard negative things about the battalion, it was from the newspapers, but I hadn't heard such things from the commander. So that was my testimony, and I stand by that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, General Petkovic, in the course of your testimony, you also said that the Vitezovi Battalion was under the direct command of Mr. Tihomir Blaskic as of January 1993, under his exclusive command?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. And there is an order -- there is a document to that effect, and that then doesn't have to do with military tasks. It has to do with all elements that relate to command. And Colonel Blaskic knows what that means.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General Petkovic, I now have another three documents for you. I'll tell you what it is about. These are reports on -- work reports for 1992, a letter from Mr. Stojic asking for a report on the basis of the decision of the HVO OHZB --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. Your Honours, I haven't been doing this regularly, and taking Mr. Karnavas counsel on board to have a -- some sort of a standing point on this, but I do think it's maybe timely to raise it again just to keep the Chamber advised of my intentions. The Vitezovi is a classic example of something that is actually brand new. It has nothing to do with Ms. Alaburic's direct examination, and again is another topic on which I'll be seeking substantial additional time, as among a number of others. This is one additional example of a brand-new topic raised on so-called cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, just a minute. A minute ago, Mr. Karnavas, when putting questions, put questions that could have to do with the joint criminal enterprise. He put questions about the interview that Mr. Prlic was in -- was involved in. I see a link there. But when you address the issue of the Vitezovi Battalion, well, what is the link? What are you trying to demonstrate? What are you trying to establish? Because if we don't understand, well, the Prosecution has an objection that they have made, and then the Judges may wonder why you are putting such and such a question. I didn't ask any questions about the Vitezovi Battalion that General Petkovic defends. Ms. Alaburic, similarly, did not address this issue. So why are you going into the subject?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, why? Well, your questions for Witness 4D-AA had to do with this subject. And as I have the right, in the course of my cross-examination, to put questions of interest for the Stojic Defence, if the witness has direct knowledge of this, and Mr. Petkovic does, as a result I wanted to confirm the allegations that Mr. Petkovic made in the Blaskic trial. This has been referred to on a number of occasions, so this is a subject of importance, in the light of your questions, too, because you referred to a document that also relates to Mr. Bruno Stojic. It was the appeal judgement in the Blaskic case. So that's why I've put this question to the witness, who can answer it directly. He can say whether he knows anything about this, whether he has any direct knowledge of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Continue. For the moment, I don't see where you're going, but a light will certainly be shed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, light will be subsequently shed, but I have now dealt with this matter. I spoke about providing reports, biannual reports from the Main Staff. I won't show you the documents, Mr. Petkovic. I don't have the time. I'll just briefly put the questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you drafted reports from the Main Staff, was the integral text, without any amendments, sent through the Defence Department to the HVO HZ-HB? And, as such, was it an integral part of the HVO HZ-HB report?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my report was a special report, a particular report. It wasn't amended in any way. First it became an integral part of the Defence Department report, and thus also an integral part of the report of the authorities of the HZ-HB. But in no way was it amended. Nothing was changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, that's what it says about the reports. For the sake of the transcript, I'll just say that the document concerned is P126 [as interpreted] and document P4699. It says that reports from the Main Staff and from the Logistics Base, because of the level of confidentiality, will be in the Office of the President of the HZ-HB. And in the second report of the president of the HVO. So that confirms that the integral text of the report was presented to the HZ-HB or, rather, to the Presidency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in the Defence Department each ministry -- in the Defence Department, each office had its reports. All the offices were in unity. The headquarters was also treated as an office of the Defence Department. But my report had to be drafted so as it didn't require any amendments, and it was in that state that it was conveyed to the Defence Department. It was part of the report of the Defence Department. No one amended it. And, as such, it was forwarded to the government or to the executive authorities of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to correct the transcript. On page 80, line 20, it's not "P126," it's P128.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's now move on to another subject. Mr. Petkovic, you said that the chief of the Main Staff, on the basis of the decision on the organisation of the Defence Department - this is document P -- we don't have to show it -- P586 - you said that he was responsible to the supreme commander with regard to issues of supreme command; organisation, strategic operative plans, and the use of the armed forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says there in that document with regard to issues that the supreme commander refers to me as the chief of staff involved in certain areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the very same decision, the chief of staff is responsible to the head of the Defence Department for all administrative affairs, for budgetary issues, and for issues that relate to materiel expenditure, and to issues that relate to the organisation of the armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's what we also said in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So according to the regulations -- according to the rules that were in force in the HZ-HB, the head of the Defence Department - I'm talking about Bruno Stojic - couldn't issue operative orders to the units of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, he couldn't if he didn't refer to Article 30 of the Decree on the Armed Forces of the HZ-HB. In certain situations, under certain conditions, that article makes it possible to command in the operative sense. The law provided that that was also possible if authority was transferred to him. So Article 30 allowed the head of the Defence Department to issue operative orders in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, do you know, as you said in your testimony, that Mr. Stojic did not have operative command? Let us leave aside what it says in the rules. You're quite right, that possibility is envisaged. But I am talking about your relationship and the head of the Defence Department. In which areas is he superior to you? Did you, in this period from 1991 until 1993 -- that is, until the 10th of November, when Mr. Stojic left the Defence Department, did he issue operative orders regarding the use of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that there were no such orders in that sense, except that there were some operative orders that were co-signed together with me. And whether the cessation of combat activities is an operative order or not, that's another matter. But as for other elements, I simply do not remember - if I'm being asked - except for orders that were co-signed by him and an order on the cessation of hostilities, which does, in a sense, contain an element of operative command, because it stops certain combat activities. I cannot recall any other documents that I had received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, it's after 12.30. We need to have our second break, and it will be the last for today. So we'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the oral decision rendered regarding Witness NO, there's something to be added on page 2. But as my pages were not numbered, I was not aware of it. The Legal Officer insists that I read these two remaining sentences. The Prlic, Praljak, and Pusic Defences, who have not filed any specific requests, will have 36 minutes to share amongst themselves for their possible cross-examination. In view of such an attribution of time for the cross-examination of Witness NO, the Chamber invites the Coric Defence to file a new schedule as soon as possible. That is a little more important. As you envisaged only one day for Witness NO, and in view of all the time that has been scheduled, it is necessary that he should come for at least two days. So make sure that the schedule is brought up to date, having noted that the person who comes following NO, who is also a protected witness, for him you had planned three days. That is what I had to say. Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, but we had changed the schedule. And for that week, as there is a free day after Witness NO, I don't know who else will have additional time, we put three 92 ter witnesses, not the second protected witness for that week. We will change the timetable, but we would be helped by a decision on the remaining two 92 ter witnesses so we can make a final timetable and things would be simpler for everyone and we wouldn't have to change the timetable every so often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Very well, thank you. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Before Ms. Nozica resumes, just to get procedural matters out of the way, because I know at 1.45 most of us are anxious, perhaps, to leave the courtroom. Your Honour, various of the Defence teams have filed a motion in terms of time -- additional time for the examination of Mr. Petkovic. There was an e-mail yesterday that I'm assure you're aware of, indicating that -- for the parties to file some sort of additional request today. Then there was a bit of -- there seems to be, and I'm not -- again, I'm not casting any blame here, but possible miscommunication or misunderstandings about that. In any event, as things currently stand, the Prosecution would ask -- obviously, the request we make depends, in part, on the timing of the other Defence of the other accused and ongoing developments, but we would ask to be able to file that motion tomorrow, rather than today, so that we can assess where things stand as of the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be allowed. I assume that Mr. Scott has not forgotten, but the request related to the time that the parties needed in connection with Judges' questions, so that how much the Prosecution will be granted should depend on Judges' questions and not on what the Defence counsel will be doing in their cross-examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. That's not my understanding. I think what the Prosecution intends to do, and we will file a motion, and of course the Chamber can handle it any way it wishes to, including denying it, but what we intend to do is to file a motion setting out our further request in the light of ongoing developments, and that includes all the additional time that's been granted to the Defence -- to the various Defence teams, additional time previously granted to Mr. -- excuse me, my apologies, Ms. Alaburic, et cetera, et cetera. So we will make one filing, additional filing, setting out what our current request is subject to further developments as they continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I have may just a word. I think that my dear colleague is practically asking for reconsideration of your decision. You delivered the decision. It is res judicata for the moment, unless he wants to appeal. Then he should ask for appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, wait a minute. I'm sorry. What about all the motions the Defence filed in the last 24 hours? Were all those motions for reconsideration as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the Prosecutor has told us that he will file a motion tomorrow, and we will see what it contains. But already, without knowing what he's going to say, the Chamber has given additional time for the cross-examination to D1, D2, D3, D5. Therefore, I assume that the Prosecutor will wish to have some additional time, too. That was my understanding. But let us wait, when we can read what he's going to write, rather than wasting time intervening now. Ms. Nozica, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to inform you that according to my calculations, I have another 24 minutes for the cross-examination. And from Mr. Pusic's Defence, I have been granted half of their time, which is another 18 minutes. So I think that will bring me to the end of this session during which I'll be able to complete my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as Mr. Pusic has granted you their time, we will finished as planned, at quarter to 2:00, so let's go on and not waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, could you give me a yes-or-no answer now. When you were the chief of staff of the Main Staff, and when you were doing other work in the Main Staff, did Mr. Stojic ever issue to you an operative order for the use of armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Your Honours, except for those two cases that I have mentioned, that I do not remember any direct order to me. This one -- I remember Praljak's, but this one, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will remind you that Mr. Praljak testified regarding this issue, and he provided an answer. My second question: Did Mr. Stojic ever issue an order to you whereby he would cease or stop your order for the use of armed forces? Please give me a yes-or-no answer.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember him giving me such an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, did you ever see any order whereby Mr. Boban transfers his authority, under Article 30, as you have said, an order by Mr. Boban where he is transferring his competencies from Article 30 to Bruno Stojic? Did you ever see such an order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether these need to be transferred or not. In the heading of those three orders, I did see Mr. Stojic referring to Article 30, so to be quite frank, I don't know whether he was given such authority or not. But there are three documents by Mr. Stojic in which he refers to Article 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, were they orders for the operative use of armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then we can move on. That is what I am interested in. Specifically with the use of armed forces, you spoke at length about the competencies of Mr. Stojic, and the Court is aware of that. Let us move on to the next topic, the method of appointment of unit commands. Could you explain to Their Honours how such appointments were made? Who made the proposals, if any? Was the Main Staff involved before Mr. Stojic made such appointments, that is, the appointments that he was authorised to make?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal regulations, Your Honours, stipulate that the chief of staff of the Main Staff may make a proposal which the head of the Defence Department accepts, and then he appoints people, or upon the proposal of the chief of staff. There were, however, individual cases when the Main Staff did sign. I, for instance, did sign, saying that I agree with the proposal coming from our brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, does that mean that proposals for appointments came from the units, from the brigades?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the brigades did provide names of people proposed for certain positions, because neither the Main Staff nor does the Defence Department have a list of available people. It was the units on the ground who would make the proposals, and then, in principle, such proposals were adopted and appointments formalised.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us now look at a document just to confirm this procedure, document P616. This is a proposal for the appointment of an officer in the Krajl Tomislav Brigade, made by Mr. Siljeg, both to the Defence Department and the Main Staff. Were the proposals usually made in this way?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the proposals coming from the units in the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, did such proposals come also for people to be relieved of their duties, that is, proposals from a unit to the Defence Department and the Main Staff, or to one or the other?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. Such proposals were also made from the lower level up, proposals for people to be relieved of duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us now look at document P2523. This is a proposal for a dismissal by Mr. Siljeg, and at the bottom I see your signature. Is that what you were referring to, that this would go to the Main Staff, and by your signature you confirm your approval?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: During your testimony, you spoke about certain dismissals and the need that you felt to initiate certain dismissals, so I would like to ask you to have a look at document 4D1038. This is a proposal for a dismissal. You have signed it. And it's being sent to the Operative Zone of South-Eastern Herzegovina. And you say: "Urgently make a proposal to the Main Staff for the dismissal from the present post in the command. Please propose how this position should be filled in and with who." Do you remember such a situation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. This was a situation in connection with the situation in Mostar, and I spoke to the commander of the operative zone. And when the conclusion was reached, that for various reasons some people need to be dismissed. And he's asked to investigate who are the people who are not fulfilling conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask Mr. Khan to switch off his microphone. We're hearing the typing. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreters perhaps can't see my microphone, but I can assure them it's off.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Document P1631.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is an exhibit. I believe you can clarify it. It is an order by Mr. Stojic to dismiss Marko Zelenika on the 9th of March, 1993. Could we please look at the document that follows. This is 3D2339. This is a report of SIS, dated the 9th of April, 1993. It's a statement by the mentioned person, Marko Zelenika, and in this statement he says that he performed various duties in the HVO. That is the first sentence after the word "Statement." That he was the commander of the Mijat Tomic Battalion in Jablanica, that he performed that duty until the 1st of March, 1993, when he took sick leave. And after medical treatment in Jablanica and Split, he returned to Jablanica. And he goes on to say in the text that upon his return, he was interviewed in the Civilian Staff, and on that occasion he declared that he would prefer to extend his sick leave in order to fully recover. He says that the someone else was put in his place, that is, Marinko Mikulic. Mr. Petkovic, can you confirm that this situation of Mr. Zelenika's sickness was the reason for him being relieved of duty?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The gentleman says that he was sick and undergoing treatment, and that, as such, he cannot hold a command position, so that some other solution has to be found for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Mr. Petkovic, is it correct to say that battalions, brigades, and operative zones, in their commands, had assistants for SIS, IPD, logistics, and the medical corps?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were a component part of the uniformed [as interpreted] service of security, and of course they did have this segment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Precisely on account of what you have just said, that they were a unified part of the SIS and IPD administrations, I have to ask you whether these assistants in the units were in the chain of command of the commander of those units, and were they given assignments from them, and were they accountable to them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain instances, yes, and in other cases they were accountable to the superior SIS body, up until the assistant head of security. So some of the work was on orders of the commanders, and a part of the work, according to their own vertical line, right up to the assistant head of security, or the SIS Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, did you ever see -- you, yourself, did you ever see any order which the head of the Defence Department or the assistant for security for IPD issued to units, commanders, or directly to assistants for these activities?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be a good idea if we had the documents of SIS, to the extent that it is available, but we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, my time is limited, Mr. Petkovic. I do have quite a number of commands of the SIS. I'm just asking you whether you saw them.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not see them, because the Main Staff does not have SIS, so it doesn't go through the Main Staff, from the SIS Administration to the brigade, or to any other lower level.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me remind you that a witness for your Defence, a Mr. Zrinko Tokic, brigade commander, on page 45458, lines 10 to 14, said, without any reservation, that these are assistants for IPD, SIS, Health and Logistics, were in the chain of command of the commander. Now, how this is according to the documents, we shall look now. Look at document 2D3083. This is an order - I assume you're familiar with it - dated the 9th of October, as it is one of your documents. I put them in chronological order to see what orders assistants for SIS and IPD received from unit commanders. And here you're sending an order to Mr. Lasic to secure facilities, and you say, in paragraph 5, that: "The formation that provides security, SIS, and the command of Sector Mostar must perform the control of the security of this facility and similar facilities as well." Does it follow from this order that you are issuing to the sector command, the SIS assistant here, an order for the tasks listed in it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, is this SIS the SIS of the brigade or the SIS Centre? But, anyway, SIS was supposed to check out the level of security of the hydroelectric power-station in this area, Salakovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From your answer, Mr. Petkovic, it follows that it could refer to the SIS Administration and the SIS Centre as well, not only the assistant in the unit?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that I cannot claim which instance of SIS this is, whether it was the commander of the operative zone or Sector Mostar, Mr. Lasic, or somebody else. So all I could do was to contact Lasic, and it was up to him, in turn, to involve and contact the SIS officials.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at P3135, which is the next order now, please. It's an order from Mr. Obradovic, and it is dated the 3rd of July. And as we can see at the bottom, it was also addressed to the chief of SIS. And in point 1, it refers to theft, the theft of property, and that proceedings should be taken through this command. In item 3, it talks about brutal behaviour, and once again that proceedings be taken through this command. In item 6, it says that the commanders, in their area of responsibility, must not allow any searches or people being taken away except by the military police and SIS in the brigade. From this, we can see that Mr. Obradovic is sending the SIS Command of the 1st Brigade an order linked to violent behaviour, theft, searches, and detention, and demands that all steps taken against perpetrators of these types of acts be done through the command. And I'm sure you've seen this document before. Does it confirm, Mr. Petkovic, what the tasks were as issued by the commander to the SIS and the military police in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is true that in the overall setup of SIS --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down, speak one at a time. And lead counsel's microphone is picking up the typing noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, because we've lost some translation here, and I'll do Judge Prandler's work. If we could have a pause, if we could have a pause. If we could speak a little slower. If for whatever reason there seems to be some typing being picked up, perhaps -- it's transferring from me, perhaps it's transferring from my desk, but we shall all endeavour to assist our good translators. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a word, it would be helpful to the translators, Ms. Nozica, if you would turn off the microphone when you do not speak, because the typing on the desk is transferred via the microphone pretty loud to the ears of the translators -- interpreters, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's rather difficult for me to keep remembering to switch my microphone on -- off.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petkovic, could you give us your answer?
